title: How to split a $5,000 dealership ad budget
excerpt: Brand, conquest and retargeting each do a different job. Most stores overspend on the one that was going to happen anyway.

title: Retargeting without following people around for six months

Cap frequency at three to five a week

title: Your vehicle detail page is the real homepage
excerpt: Search sends people to the car, not the store. Most VDPs are a template nobody has read since the site was built.

25–40 photos in the same order for every used unit
Two sentences a person wrote beat a list of option codes

title: Your lead form is asking for too much
excerpt: Name, one contact method, the vehicle. Everything past that is the store asking a stranger to do work first.
points: Name, contact method of their choice, and the vehicle
Qualify in the first reply, not on the form
Submit every form on your site yourself and check where it goes

title: Getting your dealership named when someone asks an AI
excerpt: Three or four businesses get mentioned. If yours is not one of them, nothing about that is random.
points: Make your basic facts readable on your own site

Re-check the same prompts every quarter and date the answers

title: The dealership marketing report that fits on one page
excerpt: Fourteen pages of impressions and engagement rate. Nobody reads past page two, and they are right not to.
points: Five questions on one page: leads, speed, appointments, sold, cost
Leave out anything you would not make a decision on
Cost per sold unit beats cost per lead

title: Short video that actually sells cars
excerpt: A ninety-second walkaround with wind in the mic gets four hundred views and no leads. Then the store decides video doesn't work.
points: Open on the car or the moment, not an intro
Five repeatable formats beat one big video a month
Agree approval rules once, then let the team post

title: What to do about a review you think is unfair
excerpt: Getting it removed rarely works. The six weeks spent trying are six weeks it sits there unanswered.
points: Google removes policy violations, not reviews you disagree with
The reply is for the next forty shoppers, not the reviewer
Volume and recency are the only lasting fix

title: What to actually post to your Google Business Profile
excerpt: Most dealers either post nothing or post the same inventory feed every day. Both look identical to the algorithm.
points: A profile with nothing recent looks like nobody is home
Offers, events and single real vehicles beat a daily feed
Your own photos matter more than the words

title: Why texting a lead works better than calling it first
excerpt: A call that goes to voicemail is a dead end. A text sits in an inbox until someone is ready to answer it.
points: Text first, call second
A specific first text gets answered; a canned one gets ignored
Get consent and opt-out right before you scale it

title: Facebook and Instagram ads that don't feel like a car ad
excerpt: A carousel of stock photos with a price overlay gets scrolled past in half a second. Native-feeling creative doesn't.
points: The first frame has to look like a post, not an ad
Lead ads bring volume but softer leads — plan the follow-up

title: Your website is probably too slow, and it's costing you leads
excerpt: Shoppers browse on their phones, on cellular, on the couch. Most dealer sites are slower than they will wait for — and every vendor plugin makes it worse.
points: Test on your phone, on cellular, not office Wi-Fi
Chat widgets, pop-ups and old tracking scripts are the usual culprits
Ask your provider which scripts can go, in writing

title: The best dealership content isn't made by the dealership
excerpt: A real customer's delivery photo, shared with permission, outperforms almost anything a marketing team produces on purpose.
points: Ask at delivery, when the customer is happiest
A simple signed release removes the guesswork
Repost tagged posts instead of screenshotting them

title: Your service drive sees more customers than your sales floor
excerpt: Most dealers market to conquest prospects and ignore the owners walking through the service door every day.
points: Service customers are your warmest audience
A handoff needs a daily trigger and one owner
Loyalty offers tied to service history beat conquest ads

title: Merchandising used inventory so it doesn't just sit there
excerpt: Two identical trades, priced the same. One sells in a week. The other sits for two months. The difference is almost never the car.
points: Listing quality moves days-on-lot as much as price does
A missing history report reads like something to hide
Review and re-merchandise at day 30, not day 60

title: Should you price match a competitor? The math most dealers skip
excerpt: Matching a competitor's price feels like the safe move. It's rarely the profitable one, and the math is simple once you run it.
points: Matching gives up gross on deals that might have happened anyway
Compare the deals side by side before discounting
Never publish a price-match policy
